strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-executed: achieving discrete roto-translation equivariance in a standard Transformer by (i) lifting features to functions over a Platonic-symmetry-group of reference frames, (ii) using frame-dependent RoPE positions, and (iii) replacing linear layers with group convolutions. This preserves the exact computation graph and cost of a standard Transformer (verified by matching total heads and wall-clock timings, Tables 1 and 4), which is a genuinely useful resolution of the symmetry-vs-scalability trade-off.

The theoretical analysis is sound and adds real understanding. Proposition 2 (RoPE attention as a dynamic Fourier-basis convolution with query-dependent coefficients), Corollary 1 (linear-time complexity), and the group-convolution lifting (Appendix D.3) are correct, clearly proven, and provide an insightful reframing of RoPE as learning content-adaptive geometric filters. The frequency-steering equivalence in Appendix E is a nice observation.

Evaluation breadth is a strength: the paper tests both non-equivariant tasks (CIFAR-10, ScanObjectNN) and equivariant tasks (QM9, OMol25), with careful compute-matched baselines. The ablation over groups (trivial vs C4/C6/D4 vs tetrahedral/octahedral) convincingly isolates the benefit of the geometric inductive bias, and gains over the RoPE-ViT baseline appear consistently across tasks.

Scalability is demonstrated beyond toy benchmarks: OMol25 training at a ~4x smaller compute budget yields energy MAE competitive with eSEN under matched conditions, and inference times are 2-3 orders of magnitude faster than G-Hyena/TFN while retaining equivariance.

Reproducibility is well handled: source code is attached as supplementary material, hyperparameter sweeps and training protocols are documented (Appendices G-L), theoretical results are backed by proofs, and there is an honest LLM-usage disclosure. The Fourier-domain implementation analysis (Appendix M) is a thoughtful forward-looking extension.
weaknesses: The QM9 evaluation (Table 3) reports only two properties (dipole moment µ and polarizability α) out of the standard twelve-property benchmark, and shows no error bars or multiple seeds. Claims of being 'on par with state-of-the-art' would be considerably stronger with the full property suite and variance estimates.

OMol25 results are mixed: the Platonic Transformer clearly improves energy prediction over eSEN under the matched budget but is slightly worse on forces, and the literature comparison relies on the authors' own estimated compute budgets for prior work rather than direct replication. The claim that SOTA is likely achievable with a comparable budget is speculative and deferred to future work.

The model achieves only approximate E(n) equivariance (discrete subgroups of rotations), yet some framing ('resolving the long-standing symmetry-awareness vs. scaling dilemma', 'a Platonic ideal') overstates the result. No empirical verification of equivariance error (e.g., max deviation under rotations outside G) is reported, and no analysis of how performance degrades for arbitrary rotations.

Head-to-head comparisons are limited: QM9 compares mainly against EquiformerV2, FAFormer, G-Hyena, and Rapidash on two properties; CIFAR-10/ScanObjectNN results are presented mostly as internal ablations rather than against modern task-specific baselines, so the practical significance on vision tasks is less established.

Some methodological choices rest on post-hoc justification: the constant-key design is defended through a hypothesized account of optimization instability on molecular data (Remark 1) that is plausible but not experimentally verified; the related-work appendix is a bare list of citations rather than a substantive discussion of positioning.

Minor presentation issues: typos (e.g., 'imapct', 'tetranedron'), and the standard-Transformer wall-clock baseline in Table 4 has a very large standard deviation (2.01 ± 3.74), which weakens the timing comparison.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: lifting features to functions on a finite Platonic symmetry group and combining this with frame-dependent RoPE gives a principled weight-sharing scheme that yields equivariance to translations plus a discrete rotation/reflection subgroup without changing the standard Transformer computation graph.

The theory is carefully developed: RoPE is derived from first principles as an irrep-based representation of the translation group (Appendix A), end-to-end equivariance is stated and proven (Prop. 1 / Appendix C), and the equivalence between linear RoPE attention and dynamic (group) convolution (Prop. 2, Cor. 1, Appendix D) is a genuinely useful reframing that connects attention to adaptive filters and a linear-time variant.

Evaluation spans diverse domains (CIFAR-10, ScanObjectNN, QM9, OMol25), with the equivariant vs. non-equivariant task taxonomy being a sensible experimental framing, and wall-clock timings show the method retains the cost profile of a standard Transformer.

Reproducibility is taken seriously: proofs, architecture and hyperparameter details (Appendices G–L), a supplementary code bundle, an honest Fourier-implementation throughput analysis (Appendix M), and an explicit limitation about only promising code release post-review.
The comparison to Frame Averaging (Sec. 5.3) is a meaningful contribution, showing that a natively equivariant backbone outperforms symmetrization of a non-equivariant backbone at lower cost.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence on QM9 is thin and selective: Table 3 reports only two of the twelve standard QM9 targets (µ and α), and α at 0.048 is only on par with, not better than, EquiformerV2 (0.050). Without the full property suite (e.g., εHOMO, εLUMO, ZMVE, energy U0), claims of being 'on par with state-of-the-art' are only weakly supported. No standard deviations or seed variance are reported for any main-table result, so differences like Tetrahedron (0.012) vs. Octahedron (0.010) cannot be judged significant.

There is a tension between the abstract's claims ('combined equivariance to continuous translations and Platonic symmetries... exact architecture and computational cost of a standard Transformer') and what the method delivers: equivariance only to a discrete subgroup G ⊂ SO(3), which the conclusion itself concedes is merely 'approximate E(n)'. The introduction's framing of achieving 'full roto-translation equivariance' overstates the result, and the actual positioning only becomes clear in Sections 3.3 and 5.1.

The OMol25 comparison is weakened by a heavily compute-constrained setting: the authors' own Platonic Transformer run (4 GPUs, 120 hrs) is compared against eSEN reproduced under the same budget, but the eSEN force MAE in their setting (23.92) is far from the literature value (10.11), suggesting the reproduced baseline is undertrained; conclusions drawn from this regime are not solid evidence of architectural superiority. The admission that SOTA parity would require more compute 'left for future work' concedes the main scalability claim is untested.

Key baselines are missing or weak: CIFAR-10 accuracy (~92.7%) is not contextualized against comparable modern vision transformer baselines at matched parameters, and ScanObjectNN lacks any external SOTA comparison. FAFormer is reproduced at 0.122/0.252 on QM9, dramatically worse than its published numbers, raising fairness concerns about baseline tuning (the sweep-based tuning procedure differs between the proposed method and baselines).

Remark 1 offers an elaborate speculative narrative (universal physical laws vs. statistical correlations) to explain why constant keys stabilize training on molecular data, but this is post-hoc hypothesis without ablation evidence; the mixed-kernel instability claim is itself not shown in any table or figure.

On ScanObjectNN, the model uses rotation augmentation and an identity-rotation input channel to recover global orientation information (Appendix J.2), which partially undermines the narrative that the geometric weight-sharing bias alone drives the gains; the relative contribution of this symmetry-breaking trick versus the group structure is not ablated.

Presentation issues further reduce confidence: the related-work section (Appendix B) is a bare list of method names with no discussion, and there are typographical errors ('imapct', 'weightsharing', 'tetranedron' in code identifiers) that suggest insufficient polish for a main-track submission.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: achieving roto-translational equivariance by defining RoPE attention relative to reference frames from Platonic solid symmetry groups, implemented purely as a weight-sharing/constraint scheme on a standard Transformer. This is a genuinely interesting framing of the equivariance-vs-scalability trade-off.

The theoretical development is solid and self-contained: the group-theoretic derivation of RoPE (App. A), the equivariance proof (App. C/Prop. 4), and the equivalence between RoPE attention and dynamic (group) convolution with linear-time complexity (Prop. 2, Cor. 1, App. D) are clearly stated and proven, and the convolution connection is a genuinely novel interpretive contribution.

The central efficiency claim is convincingly supported: inference wall-clock times (Table 4) show Platonic Transformer layers run at essentially the same speed as standard Transformer layers, 2-3 orders of magnitude faster than G-Hyena and TFN.

Empirical coverage is broad (2D vision, 3D point clouds, molecular property prediction at small and large scale) and includes a fair-compute comparison on OMol25 against a reproduced eSEN baseline, plus an informative comparison to Frame Averaging variants.

Reproducibility is well handled: full source code is attached as supplementary material, training details and hyperparameters are documented in Appendices G-L, and the hyperparameter tuning strategy (including matching compute between SE(n) and T(n) baselines) is transparently described.
weaknesses: The QM9 evaluation is limited to only two properties (μ and α) out of the standard 12-target benchmark suite. This selective reporting weakens the claim of being 'on par with state-of-the-art methods like EquiformerV2'; results on the full property set are needed to substantiate competitiveness on QM9.

Performance is competitive rather than state-of-the-art in most settings. On OMol25, the model falls well short of published eSEN/MACE numbers (e.g., 74.00 vs 29.80 energy MAE in literature), and the claimed outperformance is only relative to a compute-constrained reproduction; the suggestion that SOTA is achievable 'with a comparable computational budget' is speculation left to future work.

Key tables (Tables 1-3) lack error bars or seed variance, despite the appendix noting three random seeds were used for sweeps; some reported gains are small (e.g., ~1.2% on CIFAR-10, ~0.7-1.5% on ScanObjectNN), so statistical significance is unclear.

The linear-convolutional variant, advertised as a headline contribution, consistently and substantially underperforms the attention variant (e.g., 88.56 vs 91.49 on CIFAR-10; 79.8 vs 80.5 on ScanObjectNN), reducing its practical value beyond speed.

The explanation for why constant-key (purely geometric) kernels stabilize training on QM9/OMol25 (Remark 1) is an untested hypothesis presented with considerable narrative confidence; no controlled experiment isolates the cause of the reported instability.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence: 'resolving the long-standing symmetry-awareness vs. scaling dilemma', equivariance is only approximate (discrete subgroup of the continuous rotation group), and the 'no additional cost' framing requires careful caveats (e.g., heads per group element, one head minimum per frame) that are only fully explained in the appendix.

The related-work treatment (Appendix B) is unusually thin, essentially a name list without discussion, which makes it harder to precisely situate the contribution relative to steerable CNNs, RoPE-based equivariant attention, and frame-averaging methods.

strengths: Elegant and well-motivated core idea: achieving equivariance to discrete Platonic-solid symmetry groups by imposing structured weight sharing on existing linear layers and running standard RoPE attention per reference frame, thereby preserving the exact computation graph and cost of a vanilla Transformer. This directly addresses the well-known scalability problem of equivariant architectures.

Solid theoretical treatment: end-to-end equivariance is proven (Prop. 3.1, App. B), the RoPE operator is derived from group-theoretic first principles (App. A), and the formal equivalence between linear RoPE attention and dynamic (group) convolution (Prop. 4.1, Cor. 4.3, App. C) provides genuine new understanding rather than just a new module. The linear-time convolutional variant follows naturally.

Unusually broad empirical validation across non-equivariant tasks (CIFAR-10, ScanObjectNN, ImageNet-1K in App. G) and equivariant tasks (QM9 property prediction and generation, OMol25 4M, ProteinMD), with wall-clock runtime measurements (Table 11, Fig. 3) showing the claimed cost-parity and linear scaling are real.

Thoughtful ablations: equivariant vs. invariant attention scores (App. N.2), learned vs. fixed keys with an honest analysis of optimization sensitivity (App. M, Figs. 4-5), group-size vs. head-dimension trade-offs (App. F.1), equivariance error before/after training (Table 13), and a Fourier-domain implementation study (App. O).
Measured equivariance errors after training are small (0.004-0.007), and runtime results (2.8 ms vs. 44-590 ms for G-Hyena/TFN) substantiate the central efficiency claim.
Fair experimental methodology: baselines were first tuned, compute budgets matched between T(n) and SE(n) models, and hyperparameter sweep procedures are documented (App. F).
weaknesses: Reproducibility gap: the 'Open-source code:' field on page 1 is empty - no code link is provided. Although hyperparameters are extensively tabulated (Table 12), the absence of released code is a notable weakness for a paper whose practical claim rests on implementability at standard Transformer cost.

Equivariance is only to discrete subgroups of O(n), not full E(n); the paper honestly discusses this, but the title/abstract framing ('A Solid Choice For Equivariance') and some claims ('resolving the long-standing symmetry-awareness vs. scaling dilemma') overstate the achieved scope.

Some baseline comparisons are thin: on OMol25 the main comparison is against eSEN-sm (6M parameters) while Platonic models have 30-60M parameters, and CIFAR-10/Table 1 is essentially an internal ablation with no external SOTA comparison, making phrases like 'superior or competitive performance relative to task-specific SOTA methods' (Sec. 5.1) stronger than the tables strictly support.

The modest gap between DiP-{e} and DiP-Tetrahedron on QM9 generation is acknowledged but not fully explained; the discussion of whether Transformers learn equivariance without constraints remains somewhat speculative.
Head-size is fixed across ablations, so the relative contribution of geometric frames vs. feature diversity per frame is only partially disentangled (the authors concede this in App. F.1).

The dynamic-convolution result requires constant keys (k_j = 1), which performs worse than full attention by 5-6 percentage points on vision tasks; the linear-time variant's practical reach is thus narrower than the abstract implies.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: achieving subgroup equivariance by weight-sharing over Platonic solid reference frames applied to unmodified RoPE attention, with the group dimension folded into the multi-head attention axis so the architecture and cost match a standard Transformer.

The theoretical contribution is substantive and clearly presented: the connection between RoPE-attention and dynamic (group) convolution (Prop. 4.1), the linear-time corollary, the RoPE frequency-steering equivalence (App. D), and end-to-end equivariance proofs (App. B) are all given with derivations that appear correct.

Broad empirical validation across genuinely different regimes: equivariant molecular tasks (QM9 generation and regression, OMol25 4M, ProteinMD) and non-equivariant vision/3D tasks (CIFAR-10, ScanObjectNN, ImageNet-1K), with controlled compute-matched comparisons against the trivial-group baseline.

Reproducibility is above average: extensive hyperparameter tables (Table 12), tuning/selection protocols (App. F), runtime breakdowns (Table 11), equivariance-error measurements (Table 13), learned-keys stability analysis (App. M), and stated open-source code.

Honest treatment of limitations and nuances, e.g., that the validity gap between trivial and equivariant diffusion variants is smaller than in convolutional frameworks, and that Fourier-domain implementation benefits only appear at larger hidden dimensions (App. O).
weaknesses: The OMol25 comparison is the weakest link: the paper claims Platonic Transformers 'outperform a state-of-the-art architecture specifically tailored to molecular force and energy prediction,' but the baseline is eSEN-sm with 6M parameters, a deliberately small variant—not the strongest eSEN configuration or the leading OMol25 models (e.g., full eSEN, EquiformerV2-scale, MACE-family). A 60M-parameter model beating a 6M baseline does not support the SOTA framing.

Vision comparisons are internal-ablation-only: CIFAR-10 and ScanObjectNN results are compared against the paper's own trivial-group variant rather than competitive published baselines, making it hard to gauge practical significance of the reported accuracies; only ImageNet-1K (in the appendix, at 80.41% top-1 for a ViT-scale model) approaches but does not exceed contemporary reference points.

Equivariance is only approximate (restricted to subgroups of O(n)); the paper acknowledges this, but the headline framing ('A Solid Choice For Equivariance') somewhat overstates what is guaranteed for tasks requiring exact E(n) symmetry, and the OMol25 setup uses random O(3) augmentation on top, which confounds the source of the gains.

Design choices vary substantially per task (fixed vs. learned keys, QK norm, rope-on-values, learned frequencies, per-dataset hyperparameter sweeps), introducing a cherry-picking risk; the per-task justifications in App. M are helpful but the ablation coverage of these interactions is incomplete.

Molecule generation comparisons (Table 4) mix models trained under differing protocols and atom resolutions, and validity-type metrics are near saturation, limiting their discriminating power; stability metrics are more informative but baselines are from cited works rather than re-run under the same conditions.

Some central claims ('equivariance at no additional cost') rest on throughput/timing measurements that, while detailed, are limited to specific hardware and batch configurations, and the linear-convolutional variant substantially underperforms full attention (5-6 points), weakening the practical value of the headline linear-time result.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: achieving discrete roto-translation equivariance by redefining attention relative to Platonic solid reference frames, which preserves the standard Transformer computation graph and RoPE mechanism rather than adding computationally expensive equivariant modules. The framing as a principled weight-sharing scheme (group convolution structure in Eq. 7-8) is insightful.

The theoretical contributions are substantive and mostly well-supported: the group-theoretic derivation of RoPE (Appendix A), the end-to-end equivariance proposition with proof (Appendix B), the dynamic group convolution equivalence (Prop. 4.1, Appendix C), and the linear-time corollary are all coherent and add genuine understanding to why RoPE-based attention has the inductive bias it has.

The experimental program is unusually broad and largely well-controlled: CIFAR-10, ScanObjectNN, QM9 regression and generation, OMol25, ProteinMD, ImageNet-1K, with compute-matched comparisons between the trivial-group and symmetric-group variants, runtime/throughput benchmarks (Table 11), and useful ablations (heads vs. group size, learned vs. fixed keys, equivariant vs. invariant attention scores).

The paper is honest about where it is not SOTA (QM9 regression targets where PaiNN/TorchMD-NET remain stronger), distinguishes equivariant from non-equivariant task settings clearly, and includes a candid limitations section (no full E(n) guarantee, extreme scale uncharacterized). Reproducibility is aided by a complete hyperparameter table (Table 12) and detailed training protocols.

Practical significance is demonstrated at scale: on OMol25 the Tetrahedron model beats eSEN-sm on all metrics with 2.6x higher throughput, and runtime measurements support the central 'equivariance at no extra cost' claim with actual wall-clock numbers rather than FLOP estimates alone.
weaknesses: Some central claims are stronger than the evidence: 'competitive with task-specific SOTA' is asserted, but on OMol25 the only external baseline is eSEN-sm (6M params); strong scalable baselines like EquiformerV2 or the full eSEN at matched scale are not compared, which limits how conclusively the scalability claims can be verified.

The comparison logic on CIFAR-10/ScanObjectNN involves substantial parameter count differences (85.1M vs 14.2M) and hyperparameter sweeps that appear more extensive for the symmetric variants; while the authors argue compute-matching, the cleanest evidence would be more symmetric comparisons at multiple scales, and some ablations (e.g., F.1/Table 8) are described in a hedged, almost prospective manner rather than delivered as definitive analysis.

The equivariance proof of the attention block (Appendix B, Prop. B.1) is somewhat informal, e.g., glossing over exactly how RoPE terms derived from lifted positions transform under the global group action; a fully rigorous treatment of the frame-dependent RoPE score (Eq. 5) under L_R would strengthen the theoretical core.
The 'Open-source code:' link on page 1 is empty/unspecified, which undercuts reproducibility despite otherwise excellent experimental documentation.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('ProtienMD'), inconsistent labeling of lambda_E in Table 7, and a few sections (e.g., Remark 4.2's hypothesis about fixed vs. learned keys) lean on plausible-but-speculative explanations that are not fully disentangled from the empirical results.
